At a glance

The dura mater is the outer meningeal layer whose two layers form the dural folds and enclose the venous dural sinuses, including the cavernous sinus and the middle meningeal artery that supplies the dura.

Dura mater and dural folds

Source: PDF pages 72 to 73

In shortThe dura is two adherent layers that separate to enclose sinuses and duplicate to form folds.

Definition

The dura mater is the outer layer of the three meninges. It is formed of an outer and an inner layer.

The two layers are adherent to each other except at two sites:

  • They separate from each other to enclose the venous dural sinuses.
  • The inner layer duplicates (becomes double) to form the dural folds.

The three large folds

FoldShape and positionAttachmentsSinus enclosed
Falx cerebri Sickle-shaped; between the two cerebral hemispheres; has an apex, base, upper attached border and lower free border Apex: frontal crest and crista galli. Upper border: margins of the superior sagittal sulcus. Base: upper surface of the tentorium cerebelli. Lower free border rests on the corpus callosum Upper border: superior sagittal. Lower free border: inferior sagittal (in its posterior part). Base: straight
Tentorium cerebelli Tent-like; in the posterior cranial fossa between the cerebrum above and the cerebellum below; has an outer attached border and an inner free border Outer border: posterior clinoid process, margins of the superior petrosal sulcus, margins of the transverse sulcus. Inner free border surrounds the brain stem, and its anterior end crosses above the outer border to attach to the anterior clinoid process Superior petrosal sinus (petrosal sulcus) and transverse sinus (transverse sulcus)
Falx cerebelli Triangular; in the posterior cranial fossa between the two cerebellar hemispheres; has an apex, base, posterior attached border and anterior free border Posterior border: margin of the internal occipital crest. Base: lower surface of the tentorium cerebelli. Apex reaches the foramen magnum Occipital sinus (posterior border)

The two small folds

Diaphragma sellae
Circular fold covering the pituitary fossa
Cavum trigeminale
Small fold covering the trigeminal ganglion

Venous dural sinuses

Source: PDF pages 73 to 74

The dural sinuses drain venous blood and cerebrospinal fluid from the cranial cavity. They differ from veins in two ways.

Dural sinuses

  • No valves
  • Wall contains no muscle fibers

Classification

Dural venous sinuses
  • Unpaired (single)
    • Superior sagittal sinus
    • Inferior sagittal sinus
    • Straight sinus
    • Basilar plexus of sinuses
    • Intercavernous sinuses
  • Paired
    • Sphenoparietal sinus
    • Cavernous sinus
    • Superior petrosal sinus
    • Inferior petrosal sinus
    • Transverse sinus
    • Sigmoid sinus
    • Occipital sinus may be single

Superior sagittal sinus and its drainage

Source: PDF pages 75 to 76

The superior sagittal sinus begins at the frontal crest. At the base of the falx cerebri it usually curves to the right:

Superior sagittal sinus
Right transverse sinus
Right sigmoid sinus
Right internal jugular vein

The sigmoid sinus continues as the internal jugular vein in the jugular foramen. Sometimes the superior sagittal sinus curves to the left instead, forming the left transverse sinus, then the left sigmoid sinus and the left internal jugular vein.

  • The inferior sagittal sinus ends by joining the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus. The lesson then continues this route as the left sigmoid sinus and the left internal jugular vein.
  • Occasionally the superior sagittal sinus and the straight sinus unite to form the confluence of sinuses. The left and right transverse sinuses arise from this confluence, and the jugular foramen is then equal in size on both sides.
  • The arachnoid granulations are the main site of CSF drainage into the venous blood stream.

Cavernous sinus

Source: PDF pages 76 to 78

There is one cavernous sinus on each side of the body of the sphenoid. It is 2 cm long and 1 cm broad. It is traversed by fibrous tissue covered by endothelial cells, which gives it a spongy feel.

Relations

Medially
Pituitary gland, body of sphenoid and sphenoidal air sinus
Laterally
Temporal lobe of the brain
Above
Optic tract and hypothalamus
Below
Body of sphenoid and sphenoidal air sinus

Contents

The lateral wall contains four cranial nerves, arranged from above downward:

Oculomotor
Trochlear
Ophthalmic
Maxillary

The floor contains the internal carotid artery, with the abducent nerve inferolateral to it.

Tributaries

  • From the orbit: superior and inferior ophthalmic veins and the central vein of the retina.
  • From the brain: superficial middle and inferior cerebral veins.
  • From the dura: sphenoparietal sinus and middle meningeal vein.

Communications and drainage

Intercavernous sinus
Opposite cavernous sinus
Superior petrosal sinus
Transverse sinus: connects with the end of the transverse sinus or the beginning of the sigmoid sinus
Inferior petrosal sinus
Internal jugular vein: connects with its upper end

Emissary veins

Foramen ovale and emissary sphenoidal foramen
Pterygoid venous plexus
Carotid canal
Pharyngeal venous plexus
Long ophthalmic veins
Supratrochlear and supraorbital veins
Clinical relevance

Emissary veins have no valves and keep the intracranial tension constant. Blood passes in both directions according to the level of intracranial tension, so they may transmit infection from outside the cranial cavity to its interior.

Blood supply of the dura and the middle meningeal artery

Source: PDF pages 79 to 80

The arterial supply of the dura comes from variable sources, mainly the middle meningeal artery and the accessory meningeal artery. The veins of the dura follow its arteries, and the middle meningeal vein ends in the pterygoid venous plexus.

Course of the middle meningeal artery

1st part of maxillary artery
Foramen spinosum
Groove in squamous temporal bone
Anterior and posterior branches

It arises in the infratemporal fossa, enters the cranial cavity just above the middle of the zygomatic arch, and passes forwards and laterally. About 2 cm above the zygomatic arch it divides into its two branches.

Anterior (frontal) branch

  • Ascends on the inner surface of the pterion
  • Lies parallel to the central sulcus (motor area)
  • Hemorrhage may compress the motor area
  • Surface anatomy: opposite the center of the pterion, 3.5 cm behind the frontozygomatic suture and 4 cm above the zygomatic arch

Posterior (parietal) branch

  • Passes upwards and backwards towards the lambda, grooving the parietal and temporal bones
  • Runs nearly over the superior temporal gyrus (auditory area)
  • Hemorrhage may compress the auditory area
  • Surface anatomy: where a horizontal line along the supraorbital margin crosses a vertical line along the posterior border of the mastoid process

Check yourself

Which sinus is enclosed by the base of the falx cerebri?

The straight sinus.

What are the nerves in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, from above downward?

Oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary.

Through which foramen does the middle meningeal artery enter the cranial cavity?

Through the foramen spinosum, after arising from the first part of the maxillary artery.

Key Points / Quick Review

Dura and folds

  • Two layers adherent except where they enclose sinuses; the inner layer duplicates to form folds.
  • Folds: falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, diaphragma sellae, cavum trigeminale.
  • Falx cerebri encloses superior sagittal, inferior sagittal and straight sinuses.
  • Tentorium encloses superior petrosal and transverse sinuses; falx cerebelli encloses the occipital sinus.

Sinuses

  • No valves and no muscle fibers in the wall.
  • Unpaired: 5; paired: 7 (occipital may be single).
  • Superior sagittal sinus usually runs to the right transverse, right sigmoid and right internal jugular vein.
  • Confluence of sinuses: superior sagittal and straight sinuses unite.

Cavernous sinus

  • Lateral wall: oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic, maxillary; floor: internal carotid artery and abducent nerve.
  • Communicates through the intercavernous, superior petrosal and inferior petrosal sinuses.
  • Valveless emissary veins may transmit infection into the cranium.

Middle meningeal artery

  • From the first part of the maxillary artery through the foramen spinosum.
  • Anterior branch: motor area; posterior branch: auditory area.
